content.subtitulo: Orsini, Colonna, Borgia, Della Rovere, Medici and the Rome of the cardinal-nephews
content.descripcion: Kinship, offices, lordships and patronage among papal families, from Nicholas III to the reform of nepotism in 1692.

pasos.titulo: Nicholas III: Rule Rome with a family behind
pasos.texto: Giovanni Gaetano Orsini arrives at the papacy from one of the great Baronial houses in Rome. His family already has senators, castles and cardinals. As a pontiff he strengthens this network: his relatives occupy positions and accumulate resources with which they can sustain the interests of the house during his pontificate and after the next conclave.

pasos.titulo: Caetani vs Colonna: When a Family Fight Becomes Papal War
pasos.texto: Boniface VIII uses the pontificate to consolidate the Caetani; the Colonna, one of Rome’s rival families, resist. Two Colonna cardinals lose their red hats and the family fiefs are attacked. The rivalry reaches its most dramatic point in 1303, when Sciarra Colonna takes part in the attack at Anagni against the pope himself. The papacy rules Rome in close relationship with its noble clans.

pasos.titulo: Martin V Colonna: a Roman family closes the schism
pasos.texto: After decades of rival obediences, the Council of Constance elects Oddone Colonna as Martin V. The pope restores an authority recognised in the West and progressively returns the centre of government to Rome. The Colonna strengthen their connections with the Curia and regain influence over offices, resources and the city’s politics.

pasos.titulo: Piccolomini: the surname that is also inherited in the Curia
pasos.texto: The humanist and diplomat Enea Silvio Piccolomini becomes Pius II. His nephew Francesco Todeschini adopts the Piccolomini name and advances within the Church. He is elected as Pius III in 1503, although his pontificate lasts only a few weeks. Curial offices and the two popes’ patronage consolidate the family’s position.

pasos.titulo: Callixtus III opens the door of Rome to the Borja
pasos.texto: Alfonso de Borja arrives in Rome from the Crown of Aragon and, as Callixtus III, raises two nephews to the cardinalate. One of them is Rodrigo Borja. Callixtus III establishes in Rome the family network that will later favour Rodrigo Borja’s election as Alexander VI.

pasos.titulo: Sixtus IV: Cardinals, Lordships and a whole generation of nephews
pasos.texto: Francesco della Rovere employs his nephews in papal government. Pietro Riario and Giuliano della Rovere receive the cardinal’s red hat; Girolamo Riario participates in Romagna’s territorial politics. Offices, revenues and diplomatic missions strengthen a family network involved in court decisions and the pope’s projects.

pasos.titulo: Alexander VI: The Borja in Italian Politics
pasos.texto: Rodrigo Borgia is elected as Alexander VI. His children occupy prominent positions in family policy: Cesare moves from the cardinalate into warfare and territorial expansion; Lucrezia establishes marriage alliances; Juan receives Gandia and Jofré connects with Naples. Alexander’s relationship with Giulia Farnese, the future Paul III’s sister, also links the two families.

pasos.titulo: Julius II: Sixtus IV’s nephew becomes the ‘warrior pope’
pasos.texto: Giuliano della Rovere learned Roman politics within Sixtus IV’s network. As Julius II he uses warfare, diplomacy and patronage to strengthen the Papal States. Giovanni della Rovere’s marriage to Giovanna da Montefeltro connects the two families. Their descendants inherit Urbino and consolidate a territorial branch of the Della Rovere.

pasos.titulo: Leo X and Clement VII: two popes from the same Medici family
pasos.texto: Leo X is the son of Lorenzo the Magnificent and Clarice Orsini. His cousin Giulio, Giuliano de’ Medici’s son, later becomes Clement VII. The Medici connect their government of Florence with papal authority, using offices, revenues and alliances in both spheres to sustain their Italian position.

pasos.titulo: Clement VII and the Sack of Rome
pasos.texto: Clement VII allies with France against Charles V. In 1527 imperial troops reach Rome and sack the city. The pope takes refuge in Castel Sant’Angelo and is forced to negotiate. Violence and occupation weaken the papal court as the Medici’s opponents exploit the crisis to expel them from Florence.

pasos.titulo: Paul III: from Borgia kinship to Parma duchy
pasos.texto: Alessandro Farnese ascends as Paul III after a career favored, among other things, by the rise of his sister Giulia in the Rome of Alexander VI. Already pope, legitimates and promotes his descendants. His son Pier Luigi receives Parma and Piacenza; his grandson Ottavio marries Margaret of Austria, daughter of Charles V. In a generation, a papal family becomes a European dynasty.

pasos.titulo: Clement VIII: Cardinal-Nepote as Government Office
pasos.texto: With the Aldobrandini, nepotism becomes increasingly institutional. Pietro Aldobrandini, nephew of the pope, accumulates missions, rents and diplomatic responsibilities. Cardinal-nepote occupies a recognizable position within the Roman court.

pasos.titulo: Paul V and Scipione: power, wealth and a collection that will survive the pontificate
pasos.texto: Paul V quickly elevates his nephew Scipione Caffarelli, who adopts the surname Borghese. Scipione concentrates charges and heritage, but also uses that fortune to build one of Rome’s great artistic collections. Papal favor becomes political, real estate and cultural lasting capital.

pasos.titulo: Urban VIII: Barberini occupy all the squares
pasos.texto: Urban VIII promotes his brother Carlo and his three sons. Francesco and Antonio are cardinals; Taddeo concentrates secular functions and marries Anna Colonna. The wedding links two houses that centuries before competed in the streets of Rome. In the Baroque, the papal kinship already produces princes, palaces, armies and aristocratic alliances.

pasos.titulo: Innocent X: Donna Olympia and Pamphilj-Aldobrandini Merge
pasos.texto: Olimpia Maidalchini, Innocent X’s sister-in-law, exercises great influence at court. Her son Camillo is made cardinal-nephew but gives up the red hat to marry Olimpia Aldobrandini. The union brings a large inheritance into the Pamphilj family and connects the two houses’ estates and alliances.

pasos.titulo: Alexander VII: Chigi arrive in Rome
pasos.texto: Fabio Chigi had built a diplomatic career before becoming pope. After the election he calls his brother Mario and his nephews to Rome. Flavio Chigi becomes cardinal-nepote. Until then essentially Sienese family settles among the great Roman aristocracy and retains that position after the pontificate.

pasos.titulo: Innocent XI and opposition to nepotism
pasos.texto: Benedetto Odescalchi represents a twist. He gives his nephew Livio the private heritage of the family, but refuses to give him the cardinalate and limits the curial favors. The surname Odescalchi prospers, but the pope tries to more clearly separate the family fortune from the institutional resources of the Church.

pasos.titulo: Innocent XII restricts nepotism
pasos.texto: The constitution Romanum decet Pontificem of 1692 restricts nepotism and limits favours a pope may grant to relatives. Families established during earlier pontificates retain palaces, property and alliances within the Roman aristocracy. Reform changes the terms on which new papal relatives can obtain the Church’s resources and offices.

content.subtitulo: Catherine of Medici, Huguenots and the Catholic League
content.descripcion: France goes from a seemingly secure succession to four decades of religious civil war. Catherine de’ Medici tries to preserve the monarchy between the Huguenot Bourbons and the Catholic Guise until the extinction of the Valois gives the crown to the Protestant Henry of Navarre.

pasos.titulo: A Death Changes the Balance of France
pasos.texto: Henry II dies after an accident in a tournament. His son Francis II is young, married to Mary Stuart and politically dependent on the Guise, the queen’s uncles. Catherine de’ Medici moves from being the king’s wife to the mother of a vulnerable dynasty.

pasos.titulo: Catherine tries to rule between two parties
pasos.texto: Francis II dies without children and his brother Charles IX ascends the throne as a child. Catherine controls the government, but she cannot ignore either the Guise, leaders of the Catholic reaction, or the Bourbon princes of the blood who give political protection to the Reformed cause.

pasos.titulo: Wassy Turns Tension into Civil War
pasos.texto: Francis of Guise’s men attack a Protestant congregation at Wassy. Violence intensifies the confessional conflict and Louis of Condé organises a Huguenot army. Aristocratic networks mobilise troops and support around the court and religious leaders. Disputes over toleration, security and government lead to civil war.

pasos.titulo: Condé dies; Coligny inherits the Huguenot cause
pasos.texto: Condé dies in Jarnac and Gaspar de Coligny remains as the great military chief of the Protestants. On the royal side, the young Duke of Anjou, future Henry III, gains prestige. Wars begin to produce the generation that will decide the French succession twenty years later.

pasos.titulo: A dynastic wedding ends in slaughter
pasos.texto: Catherine marries her daughter Margaret to Henry of Navarre, one of the leading Huguenot princes, to strengthen the peace. Days later, the attack on Coligny and the St Bartholomew’s Day massacre destroy that strategy. Coligny dies and Henry of Navarre survives at court under enormous pressure.

pasos.titulo: Henry III returns from Poland to a broken France
pasos.texto: Charles IX dies and his brother Henry leaves the Polish crown to become Henry III of France. The Valois dynasty retains the throne, but the new king has no children and his brother Francis of Anjou is the last male heir of the family.

pasos.titulo: The death of a prince turns religion into succession
pasos.texto: Francisco de Anjou died in 1584. According to the dynastic succession, the next heir is Enrique de Navarra: a Bourbon and Protestant. Enrique de Guise reorganizes the Catholic League to prevent it and obtains support from Philip II. The War of the Three Henrys begins.

pasos.titulo: King kills man who dominated Paris
pasos.texto: The Day of the Barricades forces Henry III to flee Paris. The king seeks to regain the initiative and orders the duke of Guise’s assassination at Blois. The duke’s brother Charles of Mayenne takes over leadership of the Catholic League and maintains resistance to royal government.

pasos.titulo: The last Valois hands over the succession to a Bourbon
pasos.texto: Henry III finally allies himself with Henry of Navarre against the League, but is killed by the friar Jacques Clément. On his deathbed he recognises Navarre as his successor. Henry IV is king by dynastic right, although he must still conquer his own kingdom politically.

pasos.titulo: To win France, Henry changes confession
pasos.texto: After years of war, Henry IV embraces Catholicism. The gesture allows broad Catholic sectors to accept a Bourbon that they considered inadmissible until then. The League loses the main reason for an alternative succession.

pasos.titulo: Monarchy Survives Religious War
pasos.texto: The Edict of Nantes establishes a limited coexistence with the Protestants and closes the main phase of the wars. Catalina, Condé, Coligny and Guise have already died; the survivor is Henry IV. The reconstruction of the authority of the crown combines negotiation with both parties and the recognition of religious commitments.

content.subtitulo: The alliance that turned an Ottoman site into a European counteroffensive
content.descripcion: In 1683 a Hungarian rebellion, Kara Mustafa's offensive and Vienna's vulnerability forced Leopold I to seek help. The alliance with John III Sobieski and the princes of the Empire saved the capital and changed the sense of war in Central Europe.

pasos.titulo: A Sultan Child inherits an empire that is advancing again
pasos.texto: Mehmed IV comes to the throne at the age of six. During his long reign, the Köprülü family of grand viziers rebuilds Ottoman military and administrative capacity. As the crisis in Hungary deepens, Constantinople again turns its attention to Vienna.

pasos.titulo: Leopold I rules the most dangerous border of the Empire
pasos.texto: Leopold I is elected emperor as the Habsburgs seek to consolidate Austria, Bohemia and Hungary. His monarchy borders Ottoman territories and also faces religious and political conflicts within Hungary.

pasos.titulo: The foreign war also comes from an internal rebellion
pasos.texto: Imre Thököly leads the anti-Habsburg kuruc and accepts Ottoman support. Kara Mustafa can present the intervention as protection of a Hungarian ally, while Leopold sees an internal revolt transformed into a strategic threat to Vienna.

pasos.titulo: Leopoldo and Sobieski promise to go to each other
pasos.texto: With Innocent XI’s mediation, Leopold I and John Sobieski conclude a defensive alliance. The agreement provides for assistance against attacks on Vienna or Kraków, bringing together Polish and imperial resources to protect their positions against Ottoman advances. Negotiations connect both realms’ security and prepare military cooperation.

pasos.titulo: Kara Mustafa arrives before the allies
pasos.texto: The Ottoman army reaches Vienna in July. Leopold leaves the city and Starhemberg organises defence with the garrison. Assaults, mines and breaches threaten the walls while defenders repair fortifications and manage reserves. The relief army is still assembling and must coordinate its advance towards the besieged capital.

pasos.titulo: An Army of the Empire meets the Polish Army
pasos.texto: Charles V of Lorraine coordinates imperial troops while Bavaria, Saxony and other princes contribute troops. Sobieski crosses the Carpathians with the Poles. The relief operation brings together Habsburg monarchy, Commonwealth and Holy Roman Empire in a common force.

pasos.titulo: 12 September: the siege is broken from outside and within
pasos.texto: The Allied army attacks from the heights west of Vienna while Starhemberg maintains the city’s defense. Sobieski leads the whole and the final load of the Polish cavalry accelerates the collapse of Kara Mustafa’s positions. Vienna is liberated and the Ottoman army withdraws.

pasos.titulo: The alliance is no longer an emergency relief
pasos.texto: In 1684 Austria, Poland and Venice form a new Holy League with papal support. The allies prepare campaigns against Ottoman positions in Hungary and on other fronts. Operations require agreement over objectives, resources and cooperation among governments also defending their own interests.

pasos.titulo: The coalition captures Buda
pasos.texto: In 1686 coalition forces capture Buda. Their advance opens new positions in Hungary and strengthens Habsburg power. Subsequent campaigns of the Great Turkish War shift the frontier southeast as the allies negotiate the distribution of conquests and maintenance of their armies.

content.contexto: Site of 1683: an Ottoman offensive and a relief coalition in modern Europe, also linked to the Hungarian crisis.

content.subtitulo: How an electorate of the Empire became a great European power
Two dynastic networks that shaped Europe
